The importance of assessing self-reported HIV status in bio-behavioural 
surveys

Introduction
Community-based surveys such as population-based household and bio-behavioural surveillance surveys are primarily 
intended to assess the magnitude of epidemics of human

summary.text: Opens a 2016 Bulletin of the World Health Organization article arguing that bio-behavioural HIV surveys should ask respondents to report their HIV status, with the abstract and author affiliations. The introduction links this to measuring the HIV care cascade and progress toward the UNAIDS 90–90–90 targets, noting that many surveys fail to ask for the result of the last test. It then addresses claims that the question is too sensitive, citing refusal rates from surveys of people who inject drugs in Ukraine and men who have sex with men in Ghana. Most respondents are reported to be willing to answer.

summary.text: Argues that respondents generally do not see the HIV status question as more sensitive than other survey items, then examines the accuracy of self-reported status. Data from Malawi, Uganda, Ukraine and Kenya show varying levels of misreporting and agreement with test results. It suggests that stronger confidentiality, such as self-completed electronic questionnaires, makes truthful answers more likely.

summary.text: Continues the article by calling for research on mismatches between self-reported and tested HIV status and argues that the benefits of asking about status outweigh the risks. It explains how status questions open the way to measuring coverage of care and antiretroviral therapy, including among key populations. Table 2 gives recommendations for future surveys on staffing, interview settings, question wording, ethics, consent, confidentiality, small communities and data use. The block ends with the article's reference list.
